Why does differentiating an integral return the original function? An integral keeps a running total of the area under a curve. Now move its upper boundary by a tiny amount, dx. You add one very thin strip. Its width is dx. Its height is f(x). So the added area is approximately: f(x) × dx Divide that change in area by dx, and you get f(x). In other words: the derivative measures how fast the accumulated area is growing — and that rate is exactly the current height of the original curve. That’s the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, visually. #math #calculus #integrals #derivatives #mathematics #STEM #mathvisualization #learnmath #education #engineering

Two systems can follow the exact same rules and still end up in completely different places.  In this animation, the two pendulums begin only 0.05° apart. At first, their motion is almost identical. Then that tiny difference grows until their futures look nothing alike.  This is deterministic chaos.  Nothing random was added. The equations never changed. The only thing that changed was the starting point.  This sensitivity to initial conditions is what people usually mean when they talk about the butterfly effect: tiny differences now can become enormous differences later.  That’s the strange part of chaos theory — a system can be completely deterministic without being practically predictable.  Tiny difference. Different future.

The First Law of Thermodynamics says energy can’t be created or destroyed, only converted.  Isochoric heating (A → B) Volume locked. Heat goes in, pressure rises, temperature climbs. W = 0, so Q = ΔU.  Isothermal expansion (B → C) Temperature held constant while the gas expands. ΔU = 0, so Q = W — all the heat becomes work.  Adiabatic expansion (C → D) No heat in or out. The gas does work, so it cools. Q = 0, so ΔU = –W.  Isochoric cooling (D → A) Volume locked again. Heat leaves, pressure drops, temperature falls. W = 0, so Q = ΔU.  #physics #thermodynamics #stem #thermal #math

🌀 Same curve. Different start points. Exact same arrival time. 🤯  This is the tautochrone – the “equal‑time” curve. Drop a bead from anywhere on this cycloid, and it reaches the bottom at the exact same instant as a bead dropped from any other point.  In 1659, Christiaan Huygens proved this property and applied it to improve the pendulum clock he had invented three years earlier.  The brachistochrone (fastest descent) and the tautochrone (equal time) are the same curve – the cycloid.  Which one surprised you more – the fastest path or the equal‑time path? Where does energy actually go when two objects collide? 💥🔥  ​Here is how the Coefficient of Restitution (e) controls momentum and heat conversion:  ​• Elastic (e = 1.0): Total momentum (P = 18.0) and Kinetic Energy (KE = 54.0) are 100% conserved with zero heat generated.  • Partially Inelastic (e = 0.5): Total momentum stays 18.0, but 10.1 units of kinetic energy convert directly into heat.  • Perfectly Inelastic (e = 0.0): Objects stick together upon impact, maximizing heat loss (13.5 units) while momentum remains fully conserved.  ​Total momentum never changes—only kinetic energy converts into heat! ⚛️  ​Save this reel for your next physics exam review! 🔖  ​Follow sciencevisualised for more visual physics animations! 🚀  #sciencevisualised ​#physics  #stem #sciencereels #manim

This one looks nasty until you audit the powers: e to the two x is just e to the x squared, and e to the minus x is one over it. Multiply everything through by e to the x — safe, because e to the x is never zero — and substitute u for e to the x. What’s left is an ordinary cubic. The factor theorem finds y equals minus one, the rest factorises, and three candidates drop out. Only two survive, because e to the x is always positive, and the natural log brings back the exact answers: x equals minus log two, and x equals log three. Boyle's Law is one of the most important concepts in physics and chemistry that explains the relationship between the pressure and volume of a gas when temperature and the amount of gas remain constant. As the available volume decreases, gas molecules collide more frequently with the walls of the container, causing the pressure to increase. This inverse relationship is represented mathematically by P ∝ 1/V and the equation P₁V₁ = P₂V₂.  #physics #boyleslaw #mathematics #fyp #maths

Boyle's Law: Pressure × Volume = Constant   Push a piston down, the pressure rises. Pull it up, the pressure falls. But multiply them — and you always get the same number. That's Boyle's Law. Why is a circle’s area πr²?  Cut the circle into thin slices.  Then rearrange them:  up, down, up, down.  As the slices get thinner, the circle approaches a rectangle.  Its height is the radius:  r  Its width is half the circumference:  πr  So the area is:  πr × r = πr²  A formula almost everyone memorized — but rarely gets to actually see.  #math #geometry #pi #circles #mathematics STEM mathvisualization learnmath education
